summary: Introduces an in-band way for DNS operators to publish authenticated information about zones they serve. It lets managed DNS operators securely announce DNSSEC key parameters, even when no DS records exist yet, so the parent can set up the delegation. It updates RFC 7344 and RFC 8078.

plainLanguage.summary: A hosting company can leave a signed note for the registry saying here are my keys, so the registry can safely turn on security.

questions: what is a dsboot signaling name
how does a registry validate cds records
subtitle: How a DNS operator can publish signed hints that let a parent zone safely switch on DNSSEC for a new delegation.

tldr.problem: Securing a delegation with DNSSEC for the first time means getting the child's key parameters to the parent over a trusted channel, which is usually manual, error-prone, or checked only weakly (for example by waiting and seeing).
tldr.mechanism: The child's DNS operator copies the child's CDS/CDNSKEY records to special signal names under its own nameserver hostnames, in zones that are DNSSEC-signed. The parental agent compares these validated signals with what the child serves and, if they all match, publishes the DS records.
tldr.outcome: The parent gets a cryptographically validated, in-band way to bootstrap DNSSEC. RFC 9615 makes this the preferred method over the RFC 8078 enrollment methods and updates RFC 7344. It does not work for delegations whose nameservers are all inside the child domain.

today: RFC 9615 is a Proposed Standard from July 2024 that has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC. It updates RFC 7344 and RFC 8078, and says its method is preferred over the enrollment methods in Section 3 of RFC 8078.

sections.title: The Bootstrapping Problem
sections.content:
To turn DNSSEC on for a zone, the parent needs to publish a DS record set that points at the child's key. Getting the key information from the child to the parent has traditionally depended on who the parties are, and often involves the child DNS operator, a registrar and the registrant. RFC 7344 observed that this tends to be a manual process that is prone to mistakes, and people may avoid it altogether.

RFC 8078 automated the step: the parental agent (registry or registrar) reads the CDS and CDNSKEY records at the child's apex. For an existing delegation the child's current chain of trust can validate those records. For a brand-new one it cannot, so other means were needed: out-of-band methods, or weak cross-checks such as 'Accept after Delay'. RFC 8078 defines no in-band validation method for enabling DNSSEC.

RFC 9615 closes that gap with a generic way for a DNS operator to publish authenticated, per-zone information. DNSSEC bootstrapping is the first application. The RFC suggests others might follow, such as publishing operational metadata or API endpoints.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a lock can be put on a door, someone has to hand over the key details safely. Until now that was done by passing notes around, which is slow and easy to get wrong. This RFC gives a safer way to hand the details over.

sections.title: Signaling Domains and Signaling Names
sections.content:
The core idea is a signal: a DNS record the child DNS operator publishes under a name that the parental agent can find and validate. A signaling domain is built by putting the label _signal in front of a hostname from the delegation's NS record set. There is one signaling domain for each distinct NS target.

Each signaling domain lives in a signaling zone. If a child DNS operator implements the specification, each signaling zone MUST be signed and be validatable by the parental agent, which means it needs a valid, publicly resolvable DNSSEC chain of trust. This is typically done by securely delegating each signaling zone.

Signaling records MUST come with RRSIG records made with the signaling zone's keys. The signaling name is the child's name (without the final root label), prefixed with a label for the signaling type. For DNSSEC bootstrapping that type label is _dsboot.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine each of the hosting company's offices has a signed noticeboard. A note about your website goes on every noticeboard, and the registry only trusts notes it can prove really came from those boards.

sections.title: Publishing the Signal
sections.content:
To say it is willing to act as the child's signer, the child DNS operator MUST copublish the child's CDS/CDNSKEY RRsets at the matching signaling name under each signaling domain, except those that would fall inside the child domain. It MAY also publish them under in-domain signaling domains for simplicity, although those are not used for validation.

Unlike the records at the child's apex, a signaling RRset MUST be signed with the signaling zone's keys, and its contents MUST be identical to the RRset at the child's apex. Because this puts CDS/CDNSKEY records at names below the apex, the RFC also says there MUST NOT be a zone cut at a signaling name, to rule out any semantic collision. For this purpose, the first bullet ('Location') of Section 4.1 of RFC 7344 is removed.

The RFC's example child is example.co.uk with NS records ns1.example.net, ns2.example.org and ns3.example.co.uk. The required signaling names are _dsboot.example.co.uk._signal.ns1.example.net and _dsboot.example.co.uk._signal.ns2.example.org. Nothing is required under the in-domain _signal.ns3.example.co.uk.
sections.plainLanguage: The hosting company pins a signed copy of the website's key details to each of its outside noticeboards. It does not bother with a board that belongs to the website itself, because nobody can trust that one yet.

sections.title: How the Parent Validates and Reacts
sections.content:
The parental agent, knowing the child name and its NS hostnames, MUST run four steps. Step 1: check that the child has no DS records at the parent and that at least one nameserver is outside the child domain. Step 2: query the CDS/CDNSKEY RRset at the child apex directly from each authoritative server in the parent-side NS RRset, without caching. Step 3: query the RRset at the signaling name under each out-of-domain signaling domain, using a trusted resolver and enforcing DNSSEC validation. Step 4: check, separately by record type, that everything from Steps 2 and 3 is equal.

If all steps pass, the parental agent can publish the DS RRset, with the precautions in Section 5 of RFC 8078. It MUST abort on any error: the child already being securely delegated or having only in-domain nameservers, any retrieval failure, a failed DNSSEC validation or missing AD bit, or any mismatch, including an RRset that is empty in one place and non-empty in the other.

Parental agents SHOULD start this procedure when they see a new or updated NS RRset, get a notification from the child, find a signaling record during a scan, an NSEC walk or a zone transfer, or hit another condition set by local policy. Timer-based scans scale poorly, so on-demand triggers such as notifications are preferred.

When a list of bootstrappable domains comes from somewhere other than the parent, the agent MUST NOT assume the nameserver where it saw a signal is really authoritative for that child. It MUST check that the delegation contains that hostname and query only the nameservers listed in the parent's delegation.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry asks the website directly, then checks the signed noticeboards, and only if every answer says exactly the same thing does it turn the lock on. If anything is different or missing, it stops.

sections.title: Limits and Operational Advice
sections.content:
Because of Step 3, bootstrapping does not work for fully in-domain delegations, since no chain of trust to the child exists yet. As a workaround, an out-of-domain nameserver can be added to the initial NS RRset and removed after bootstrapping; RFC 7477 CSYNC records can automate this. Signaling names must also be valid DNS names, so the label count and length limits of RFC 1035 mean unusually long child domains or NS hostnames do not work.

For child DNS operators, the RFC notes that CDS/CDNSKEY and signaling records can be added without the domain owner's explicit knowledge, so operators are advised to tell owners, for example in a GUI at zone creation or by email. When moving a zone between operators, the two should cooperate, for example using the multi-signer protocols of RFC 8901. Signaling domains SHOULD be delegated as standalone zones, and processed signaling records should be removed to keep the zone small.

For parental agents, it is RECOMMENDED to query signaling domains with an initially empty resolver cache, to avoid stalemates from stale cached records in Step 4. It is also RECOMMENDED to use QNAME minimization (RFC 9156) for signaling lookups.
sections.plainLanguage: The trick does not work if all of a website's helpers live on the website itself, because there is no outside board to check. Everyone is also told to be open about what they are doing and to tidy up old notes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The method builds on the approaches in Section 3 of RFC 8078 but adds authentication, so the RFC says its security level is strictly higher than those approaches, such as 'Accept after Delay'. Otherwise the same security considerations apply as in RFC 8078.

The rigor in Step 2 to Step 4 is there to prevent publishing a DS RRset that only some of the NS hostnames agreed to. For example, in a setup with several operators, one operator cannot enable DNSSEC unless all the others agree. Because the child DNS operator knows the child's real CDS/CDNSKEY records, it can readily detect fraudulent DS provisioning.

To avoid the parents of the nameserver hostnames becoming a single point of failure, the RFC advises diversifying the path from the root to those hostnames, for example by using different, independently operated TLDs. Without QNAME minimization, an upstream parent of a signaling domain would see the CDS/CDNSKEY queries and could answer with its own signed answer instead of a referral, so using it reduces the forgery attack surface.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the registry insists that every noticeboard agrees, one dishonest board cannot trick it. It is also wise to keep the boards in different places so one problem cannot break everything.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA has added two entries to the 'Underscored and Globally Scoped DNS Node Names' registry from RFC 8552: the RR types CDS and CDNSKEY, each with the node name _signal, referencing RFC 9615.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of reserved name tags now includes the _signal tag for these two kinds of record, so nobody else uses it for something different.
